source.title: Zeroth-Order Optimization Finds Flat Minima
source.authors: Liang Zhang; Bing-Cong Li; K. Thekumparampil; Sewoong Oh; M. Muehlebach; Niao He

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own results on a related sharpness measure and test accuracy, but it does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap relation specified in V7. It finds trace of Hessian decreases under zeroth-order optimization while test accuracy is comparable to gradient descent in the convex classification tasks; this refines the scope of the related sharpness claim.
record.gate_note: The paper measures trace of Hessian and test accuracy during optimization. Its figures do not provide recoverable numerical values in the supplied text, so only the explicitly stated qualitative outcomes are recorded. It does not test random-label memorization, width, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, optimizer generalization gaps, batch-size effects, dropout, or memorized-example removal.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether zeroth-order optimization reduces Hessian trace, not any listed claim version. Its unscaled Hessian trace and isotropic expected-sharpness estimate do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of training–test gaps. GD versus zeroth-order optimization also does not test V4's adaptive-optimizer comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors establish implicit Hessian-trace regularization and convergence to approximate flat minima for convex, sufficiently smooth objectives, with supporting classification and RoBERTa experiments. They do not establish that magnitude-aware sharpness tracks generalization gaps.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares zeroth-order optimization with gradient descent on convex binary classification and RoBERTa fine-tuning tasks; it does not use the interventions or measurements in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The smoothing parameter λ controls the trace-regularization and optimization-error trade-off in the illustrative test function. Results are reported across datasets, few-shot sample counts, and random seeds; the paper says the qualitative results are consistent across three seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: On a5a and w5a SVM and logistic-regression tasks, zeroth-order optimization reduces Hessian trace while ultimately achieving training loss and test accuracy comparable to GD (Section 4, Figures 2 and 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Zeroth-order optimization can reduce unscaled Hessian trace without improving held-out accuracy relative to GD on these convex classification tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: During RoBERTa-Large few-shot fine-tuning, both methods reduce estimated Hessian trace; GD usually achieves lower training loss, smaller estimated trace, and higher test accuracy (Figure 3). The estimate uses isotropic perturbations and 100 samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GD and zeroth-order optimization both reduce isotropic expected sharpness in the tested language-model fine-tuning settings, with GD usually performing better on all three reported measures.

fits_no_version.finding: The convergence theorem guarantees approximate minimum-Hessian-trace solutions under convexity and higher-order smoothness assumptions; the illustrative function shows a smoothing-dependent trade-off between trace reduction and optimization error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The standard two-point zeroth-order estimator implicitly favors small Hessian trace, with convergence guarantees under the stated assumptions.

record.problems: The neural-language-model trace is an approximation based on expected sharpness and 100 samples, not an exact Hessian trace. The relevant plots provide qualitative outcomes but no recoverable numerical values in the supplied text. The experiments do not directly measure training–test gaps or test whether sharpness ranks those gaps.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible version-specific rows: the results do not measure the specific behaviors named by V1–V8. Results on trace of Hessian and test accuracy are captured under fits_no_version, but no rows are added because the supplied text presents the plotted outcomes without recoverable per-condition values.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and its ranking relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the record's tests/T5 classification and V7 tested_not_extracted status: no listed version is tested. Full-batch training is used to suppress minibatch noise, not to compare batch sizes. Empty version-specific rows and verdicts are appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization by the same architectures and recipes.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and their test-error effects.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization comparisons.
Large versus small batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.

The paper measures trace of Hessian or its expected-sharpness approximation, not magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance; it does not compare networks of one convolutional family at similarly low training loss or assess how that measure ranks training–test gaps. Its reported outcomes are recorded under fits_no_version.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
